lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: How tall is that mountain? How far out is that ship? How far away is the Moon?

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: You can't stretch a tape measure to any of them.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: But you can stand on the ground, measure a couple of angles and one distance, and work out the rest.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: That need is what gave us trigonometry.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: The name comes from two Greek words: trigonon, a triangle, and metron, a measure.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: Trigonometry literally means measuring triangles.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: The core idea is this. If you know enough about a triangle, say one side and two angles, then every other side and angle is already decided.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: And since almost any shape can be cut into triangles, measuring triangles means measuring almost anything.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: The first people to lean hard on this tool were astronomers.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: Hipparchus, a Greek astronomer who lived more than two thousand years ago, is usually credited with the first trigonometric table we know of.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: His original is lost. We know it mostly through writers who came centuries later, like Ptolemy.

lines.act: ACT ONE — Measuring the unreachable
lines.text: So from the very start, trigonometry was about the sky and enormous distances, not little triangles on a worksheet.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Here's the step that most of us skipped in school.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Pick an angle, say thirty degrees. Build a right triangle with that angle, and divide the side opposite it by the longest side, the hypotenuse.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: You get one half.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Now build another right triangle with the same thirty-degree angle, twice as big. Or ten times smaller.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Divide again. One half. Every single time.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: The reason is that these triangles are similar. Same angles, same shape, only the size is different.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: And when you scale a shape up or down, every ratio between its sides stays exactly the same.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: So that ratio doesn't care which triangle you drew. It only depends on the angle.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Every angle carries its own fixed number. For thirty degrees, it's one half.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: That number is what we call the sine of the angle.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: In the same way, the cosine is the adjacent side over the hypotenuse, and the tangent is the opposite side over the adjacent one.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Three fixed numbers, attached to every angle.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: And the name has a strange history.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Indian astronomers called it jya, the bowstring: the straight string stretched across a bent bow, like a chord across an arc of a circle.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Arabic scholars wrote the word as jiba, and since Arabic is written without vowels, later readers took it for jayb, a fold.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Latin translators turned that fold into sinus. And sinus became our sine.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Notice what that bowstring was. Not the side of a right triangle, but a chord, inside a circle.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Even Hipparchus's table, as far as we can tell, was a table of chords in a circle.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: So here's the first answer. Every angle has one sine because similar triangles keep their ratios.

lines.section: A number that belongs to the angle
lines.act: ACT TWO — One number for every angle
lines.text: Which means sine isn't really a rule about triangles. It's a function: you give it an angle, and it gives you back one number.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Stuck below ninety
lines.text: But the triangle definition has a limit you hit very quickly.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Stuck below ninety
lines.text: In a right triangle, the other two angles are always between zero and ninety degrees.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Stuck below ninety
lines.text: So what is the sine of one hundred and twenty degrees? Of minus thirty degrees? Of an angle bigger than a full turn?

lines.act: ACT THREE — Stuck below ninety
lines.text: With opposite over hypotenuse, those questions don't even make sense. There is no right triangle with a one-hundred-and-twenty-degree angle.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Stuck below ninety
lines.text: You might think that's fine, since triangles are what trigonometry was made for.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Stuck below ninety
lines.text: But the world is full of angles like that. A wheel doesn't stop turning at ninety degrees. Anything that swings or spins passes through every angle there is.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Stuck below ninety
lines.text: If sine only worked from zero to ninety, it would be far too weak to describe any of it.

lines.act: ACT THREE — Stuck below ninety
lines.text: We need a definition that works for every angle at all. And the most natural one comes from a circle.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: Draw a circle with a radius of one, centred where the two axes cross. It's called the unit circle.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: Put a point on the circle, and measure its angle starting from the axis pointing right, turning counter-clockwise.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: Now here is the new definition. The point's horizontal position, its x coordinate, is the cosine of the angle.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: Its height, its y coordinate, is the sine.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: Cosine tells you how far left or right the point is. Sine tells you how high or low.

lines.section: The old sine is still inside
lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: First, let's check that nothing broke.

lines.section: The old sine is still inside
lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: For an angle between zero and ninety, drop a line from the point straight down to the axis.

lines.section: The old sine is still inside
lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: You get a right triangle, and its hypotenuse is the radius, which is one.

lines.section: The old sine is still inside
lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: So opposite over hypotenuse is just the height divided by one. The old sine and the new sine are the same number.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: Now let the point keep going.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: At one hundred and twenty degrees, it's past the top, over on the left. Its height is zero point eight six six.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: That's the number your calculator gave you.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: At minus thirty degrees, you turn the other way, clockwise, and the point sits below the axis, at minus one half.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: And a thousand degrees? That's two full turns, and two hundred and eighty degrees more.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: The point lands low on the right, at about minus zero point nine eight five.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: Big angles, negative angles, angles that wind around many times. Every one of them is just a point somewhere on the circle.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The unit circle
lines.text: That's the second answer. Your calculator isn't looking for a triangle. It's finding a point on a circle.

lines.section: Three hundred and sixty is a choice
lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: Degrees are so familiar that we forget they were a choice.

lines.section: Three hundred and sixty is a choice
lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: A full turn is three hundred and sixty degrees probably because of the Babylonians, who counted in sixties.

lines.section: Three hundred and sixty is a choice
lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: Three hundred and sixty splits neatly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths and many more, which is handy.

lines.section: Three hundred and sixty is a choice
lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: But there's nothing special about it mathematically.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: Radians measure an angle with the circle itself.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: Take the length of the arc that the angle cuts out, and divide it by the radius.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: A circle's circumference is two pi times its radius, so a full turn is two pi radians.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: Half a turn, one hundred and eighty degrees, is pi. A quarter turn is pi over two.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: On the unit circle, where the radius is one, the angle in radians is exactly the distance the point has travelled along the circle.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: The angle and the distance become the same number.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: That makes a lot of formulas cleaner.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: The rate at which sine changes is exactly cosine. In calculus language, the derivative of sine is cosine.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: But that's only true in radians. Measure in degrees, and an awkward extra factor, pi over one hundred and eighty, sneaks into every formula like it.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why mathematicians measure in radians
lines.text: That's why mathematicians and scientists switch to radians, and stay there.

lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: This is where trigonometry turns from geometry into the language of physics.

lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: Picture a point running around the unit circle at a steady speed.

lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: Now ignore everything except its height, the sine, and plot that height as time goes by.

lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: The horizontal axis is the angle, which you can also read as time. The vertical axis is the sine.

lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: What you get is a smooth line rising and falling. Up to one, down to minus one, and up again, forever.

lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: That's the sine wave.

lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: The cosine wave is exactly the same shape, just shifted by a quarter of a turn.

lines.section: A circle seen from the side
lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: Here's what I most want you to keep.

lines.section: A circle seen from the side
lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: That wave is circular motion, seen from the side.

lines.section: A circle seen from the side
lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: Anything that turns steadily, viewed edge-on, moves back and forth in a sine wave.

lines.section: A circle seen from the side
lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: A pendulum making small swings. A vibrating guitar string. The alternating current in your wall socket, turning fifty or sixty times every second.

lines.section: A circle seen from the side
lines.act: ACT SIX — The circle becomes a wave
lines.text: That's the third answer. Sine and cosine turn up everywhere, because steady turning turns up everywhere.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: Trigonometry has a reputation for endless formulas to memorise. But most of them fall straight out of the circle.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: Take the famous one: sine squared plus cosine squared equals one.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: On the unit circle, every point is at a distance of one from the centre. That's what a circle of radius one is.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: By Pythagoras, that circle's equation is x squared plus y squared equals one.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: Put cosine in place of x and sine in place of y, and there it is. Sine squared plus cosine squared equals one.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: It's just the circle, written in the language of trigonometry.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: The others work the same way.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: Why does sine repeat every full turn? Because the point comes back to where it started.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: Why is the sine of a negative angle minus the sine? Because turning the other way mirrors the point below the axis.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: The addition and double-angle formulas come from turning a point twice in a row.

lines.act: ACT SEVEN — The formulas are just the circle
lines.text: Keep the circle clear in your head, and the formulas stop being a list to memorise. They become things you can see.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: So how did a tool for solving triangles end up underneath modern science?

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: The key is repetition. So much of nature repeats in a rhythm.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Sound is air being pushed back and forth. Light and radio are oscillations of electric and magnetic fields.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Alternating current, the tides, the seasons coming round every year.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Anything that repeats steadily like that can be described with sine and cosine.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: In the early eighteen hundreds, the French mathematician Joseph Fourier went much further.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: He showed that almost any repeating pattern, however messy, can be built by adding up simple sine waves.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: That one idea is inside your phone when it compresses music, inside an MRI scanner building a picture of your body, and inside the signals that carry your mobile data.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Trigonometry started out measuring the world. It ended up as the language of everything that turns and vibrates.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Every angle has one fixed sine, because similar triangles keep their ratios.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Your calculator can answer sine of one hundred and twenty degrees, because sine is the height of a point on a circle, and every angle lands somewhere on it.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: And that circle hides inside every wave, because a wave is steady turning, seen from the side.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: If you remember one thing from this video, let it be this picture.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: A point running around a circle. Cosine is how far across, sine is how high, and the angle is the distance it has travelled.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Let it run, and sine and cosine ripple out into waves.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Next time you see a ripple, a swing, or a vibrating string, try to picture the circle turning behind it.

lines.act: ACT EIGHT — Everything that repeats
lines.text: Thanks for watching all the way to the end. If you enjoyed this, leave a like and subscribe, so you don't miss the next one. See you then.
